title: Efficient Block Encodings for Ensembles of Molecular Hamiltonians
authors: Cristian L. Cortes, Andrew J. Jenkins, William Pol, Dario Rocca, Mark Steudtner, Gian-Luca R. Anselmetti, Matthias Degroote, Nikolaj Moll, Raffaele Santagati, Michael Streif, Markus R. Hermann
abstract: Accurately characterizing molecular properties and reactivity often requires electronic-structure calculations across an ensemble of molecular geometries. Quantum algorithms that process such ensembles coherently could address this challenge, but they require Hamiltonian block encoding circuits that combine advanced factorization techniques with sublinear scaling in ensemble size. Here, we introduce SVD-THC, which extends tensor hypercontraction to sets of Hamiltonians defined at different nuclear geometries through a singular value decomposition of the ensemble. We use SVD-THC to construct a single multiplexed block encoding circuit for all geometries in an ensemble. We then evaluate the approach on ensembles generated by varying internal rotational coordinates in 1-bromo-2-chloroethane as well as in glycine and alanine dipeptides, corresponding to established model systems for peptide conformational landscapes, with up to 5,184 geometries. Across several resolutions of the internal-coordinate grids, the Toffoli complexity of the resulting circuits grows only weakly with the number of geometries, changing by at most 12\% over grids that differ in size by up to 576$\times$. In an energy-thresholding circuit, this yields 35--200$\times$ fewer Toffoli gates than slicing together single-geometry block encodings. This approach could help make coherent processing of molecular geometry ensembles a useful primitive for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
summary: This paper introduces SVD-THC, a novel technique to efficiently encode molecular Hamiltonians defined over large ensembles of geometries. By using Singular Value Decomposition, it compresses the required quantum circuit size, leading to massive reductions in the number of required quantum gates compared to state-of-the-art methods. This makes coherent processing of molecular conformational landscapes feasible for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: Developing quantum algorithms to process electronic structure calculations across an ensemble of molecular geometries coherently, which requires highly efficient Hamiltonian block encoding circuits.
main_result: The proposed SVD-THC method constructs a single multiplexed block encoding circuit whose Toffoli complexity grows only weakly with the number of geometries, yielding massive reductions in required quantum gates compared to naive methods.
method: The core method is SVD-THC, which uses Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to compress the ensemble of geometry-dependent Hamiltonians into a superposition of a small number of geometry-independent mode Hamiltonians.
model_or_system: The system involves molecular Hamiltonians parameterized by internal rotational coordinates (e.g., in 1-bromo-2-chloroethane or dipeptides), forming an ensemble over a product grid of geometries.
key_observables: Toffoli complexity, Toffoli gate counts, and the compression factor (e.g., 35–200x reduction in gates).
important_parameters: The scaling must be sublinear in the ensemble size ($o(M)$), and the energy accuracy must be maintained (e.g., CCSD correlation energy within $0.6 	ext{ mHa}$).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that the ensemble of Hamiltonians exhibits significant redundancy, allowing for effective compression via SVD.
figures_summary: Figures compare resource estimates (Toffoli gates) for different quantum phase estimation approaches (SVD-THC vs. sequential/sliced QPE) across various molecular systems.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of ensemble encoding, details the SVD-THC technique by expanding the Hamiltonian into mode Hamiltonians, and then rigorously compares the resource scaling (Toffoli gates) against established methods using molecular model systems.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, resource-aware quantum primitive for simulating complex molecular dynamics, directly addressing the scaling bottleneck in quantum chemistry simulations.
